easy.heading: Waking Up With A Quick Win
easy.body:
I started my morning with the easy grid and it was such a nice way to get the brain moving. I first looked at the spots that needed to be greater than 5, specifically at (2,0) and (2,3). Since our dominoes today included [4,6] and [6,2], I knew those 6s had to go in those spots. I placed the [2,0] domino vertically so the 6 landed right on that (2,0) constraint, and did the same with the [3,3] and [2,3] domino to get the 6 onto (2,3).

Next, I looked at the bottom right where a group of three cells at (3,3), (4,2), and (4,3) had to add up to 8. I already had a 2 in the (3,3) spot from my previous move, so I needed the other two cells to add up to 6. Using the [4,2] domino there worked perfectly. It felt great to see the bottom of the board click into place so fast! The rest was just matching up the equals signs, like putting the [1,1] domino in that top left section.

medium.heading: Navigating The Empty Spaces
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt a bit like a ghost town because of all those empty cells! I had to be careful not to let my dominoes land on (1,0), (2,0), or (2,3). I focused my attention on the sum constraints first. I saw that (4,0) needed a sum of 5, but it was only one cell. That meant the half of the domino landing there had to be a 5. I used the [5,1] domino, which placed a 5 at (4,0) and a 1 at (3,0). Since (3,0) had to be less than 4, that 1 fit just fine.

Then I tackled the middle section. There was another sum of 5 at (3,2) and (4,2). I used the [2,3] domino to fill those, which felt like a solid choice. The hardest part was figuring out where to put the big [6,6] domino since it couldn't go near any of the less than 4 areas. I eventually found a home for the remaining pieces by matching the equals constraints at (0,2) and (1,2). It took a minute of shuffling, but once the 5s and 0s were placed, the rest flowed naturally.

hard.heading: Tackling The Big Grid Giant
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today really made me work for it! With fourteen dominoes to place, I felt a little lost at first. I decided to hunt for the greater than 4 constraints because those are usually the most restrictive. Looking at (1,2), (4,4), and (8,4), I knew I needed to save my 5s and 6s for these spots. I placed the [6,6] and [6,5] dominoes early on to satisfy the requirements at the top and bottom. 

One of the biggest breakthroughs was the equals region at (2,2), (3,2), and (4,2). Since three cells had to be identical, I had to find dominoes that could share a value across those boundaries. I used parts of the [2,2] and [0,2] dominoes to make it work. The bottom left corner was a bit of a mess for a second because of the less than 3 constraints at (8,1) and (9,1). I had to swap my [1,0] and [0,0] dominoes a few times before I realized I was blocking myself. Once I settled on putting the [1,1] pair down there, everything else finally aligned. It was a long solve, but seeing that final checkmark was so satisfying!

explanation.tips: Try to look for the greater than or less than constraints first because they really limit which dominoes you can use in those specific spots. If you get stuck, look for the equals regions that cover three cells instead of two, as those are usually the anchors for the whole puzzle. Don't be afraid to pull a domino back off the board if a sum isn't working out; sometimes you just need to flip it around!
explanation.learned: Today I learned that empty cells can actually be your best friends because they act like walls that guide where dominoes must go. I also noticed a pattern where the largest dominoes, like the [6,6], are almost always tucked away into the greater than regions or large sum areas, which helps narrow down the search area significantly. It really pays to scan the whole list of available dominoes before making your first move to see if any high-value ones are required for specific sums.

faqs.question: What does the empty square mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty square is a constraint that means no domino can be placed on that specific cell. You have to work your dominoes around these gaps.

faqs.question: How do you solve the sum constraints in Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum constraint shows a number that the cells inside the outlined region must add up to. You need to pick dominoes whose pips total that exact target number when placed in those spots.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes can only be placed horizontally or vertically to cover two adjacent cells on the grid.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for the hard level of Pips?
faqs.answer: Start with the most restrictive constraints like greater than 5 or sums that require specific high or low numbers. Once the corners and edges are filled, the middle usually becomes much easier to solve.

faqs.question: Are all dominoes from a standard set used in every puzzle?
faqs.answer: The game provides a specific list of dominoes for each puzzle, and you must use all of the ones listed in the tray to complete the grid.
